Chronically online
KRON-ik-lee on-LYNE
adjective phrase (Gen-Z slang)
From chronic (Greek chronos, time; of lasting illness) and online. The phrase became a common Twitter and TikTok put-down around 2020–2021, during pandemic lockdowns: a person so immersed in internet culture that his opinions, references, and outrage no longer match how ordinary people think and live. Close kin: "touch grass" (go outside).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang a person is chronically online when the internet has become his world: his jokes need three memes of context, his outrage is about things no one offline has heard of, and his sense of normal comes from a feed. Gen-Z uses it as an insult and, increasingly, as a confession. The Christian observation: the phrase is a diagnosis about time. Scripture tells believers to "walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:15–16), and Moses prays, "teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12). Hours poured into a feed are days unnumbered. David’s resolution reads like a screen-time policy: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). And the slang’s deeper insight is about the mind being shaped by what it consumes; Paul says, "be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). A chronically online mind has been conformed by an algorithm. A father tells his son: go outside, read a book, sit at a real table, work with your hands; set your affection on things above (Col 3:2), and let God’s Word, not your feed, tell you what is normal.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (Twitter / TikTok, c. 2020–2021) for one so immersed online that his sense of reality is warped — a diagnosis of unredeemed time and a conformed mind.

expand to see more

CHRONICALLY ONLINE, adj. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present) So immersed in internet culture as to lose touch with ordinary offline life. "That take is so chronically online."

Used of people, opinions, jokes, and outrage. Often paired with "touch grass."

Also self-applied: "I’m chronically online, I know."

Webster (1828), root word chronic: “CHRONIC, CHRONIC AL, adjective Continuing a long time, as a disease. A chronic disease is one which is inveterate or of long continuance, in distinction from an acute disease, which speedily terminates.”

Decode for parents: your child’s own generation has named the problem. Help him act on the diagnosis.

Eph 5:15 — "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,"

Eph 5:16 — "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil."

Psa 90:12 — "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

Psa 101:3 — "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me."

Modern Corruption

Chronically online diagnoses a mind formed by the feed and days spent unnumbered; Scripture prescribes redeeming the time and a mind renewed by God, not conformed to an algorithm.

expand to see more

Unusually, this is the culture correcting itself. Young people coined the phrase because they could see what endless scrolling does: it shrinks the world to a feed and makes the feed feel like the world. The opinions it produces are not merely wrong but unreal — outrage at strangers, contempt for ordinary life. Paul’s word for the process is conformity: the mind pressed into the shape of "this world" (Rom 12:2).

Scripture’s remedy is stewardship of time and of the eyes. "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16); "teach us to number our days" (Psa 90:12); "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). Turn your child’s own diagnosis into a family practice: phones away at the table, books and work and church in their place.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek chronos (time) → chronic, lasting → + online → c. 2020–2021 Twitter / TikTok put-down for internet-warped people and opinions.
